subject: chem
title: States of Matter
subtitle: Ideal gases, kinetic theory, and intermolecular forces in liquids and solids.
concept: The kinetic theory of gases assumes ideal gas behaviour: negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces, elastic collisions.
PV = nRT relates pressure, volume, moles and temperature for an ideal gas. Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
Intermolecular forces determine the physical state and properties of substances.

notes.heading: Kinetic Theory of Gases
items: An ideal gas obeys the assumptions of kinetic theory: (1) gas molecules have negligible volume compared to the container; (2) there are no intermolecular forces between them; (3) all collisions are perfectly elastic (no kinetic energy lost); (4) the average kinetic energy of the molecules is proportional to the absolute temperature (T in K).

Pressure arises from the constant bombardment of the container walls by gas molecules. Increasing temperature increases the average kinetic energy and therefore the frequency and force of collisions — pressure rises at constant volume.

notes.heading: Gas Laws and the Ideal Gas Equation
items: Boyle's law: at constant T and n, P ∝ 1/V (PV = constant). Charles's law: at constant P and n, V ∝ T (T must be in K). These combine into the ideal gas equation: PV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, P in Pa, V in m³, T in K.
Molar volume at RTP (25 °C, 100 kPa): 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹.

notes.heading: Real vs Ideal Behaviour
items: Real gases deviate from ideal at high pressure (particle volumes are no longer negligible) and low temperature (intermolecular forces become significant — they reduce the pressure below the ideal value at moderate distances).
Noble gases and H₂ behave most ideally at room temperature and pressure.

definitions.body: A gas that obeys PV = nRT under all conditions; assumes negligible particle volume and no intermolecular forces.
At constant temperature and amount, the pressure of an ideal gas is inversely proportional to its volume: PV = constant.
At constant pressure and amount, the volume of an ideal gas is proportional to its absolute temperature: V/T = constant.

workedExamples.q: Calculate the pressure exerted by 0.500 mol of gas in a 10.0 dm³ container at 300 K.

mistakes: Using temperature in °C instead of Kelvin in gas law calculations — always convert: K = °C + 273.
Using dm³ in the ideal gas equation when the equation requires m³ (unless using P in kPa).
Stating that melting a covalent solid breaks covalent bonds — for simple molecular solids, only intermolecular forces are overcome.
tips: Convert to SI units first: Pa (pressure), m³ (volume), K (temperature).
To avoid unit confusion: PV = nRT in Pa and m³, OR PV = nRT in kPa and dm³ (same R value works in kPa·dm³).
Real gas deviations: remember 'high P and low T' favour real-gas behaviour.

flashcards.a: PV = nRT (P in Pa, V in m³, T in K, R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)

flashcards.q: What are two conditions where real gases deviate most from ideal behaviour?
flashcards.a: High pressure (particle volume significant) and low temperature (intermolecular forces significant).
At constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume: PV = constant.

flashcards.q: What is the kinetic theory assumption about molecular collisions?
flashcards.a: All collisions are perfectly elastic (no kinetic energy is lost).

flashcards.q: What happens to gas pressure if volume is halved at constant temperature?

questions.q: What volume (m³) does 2.00 mol of ideal gas occupy at 100 kPa and 27°C?
A gas is at 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 4.0 dm³. If volume halves at constant T, what is the new pressure?
questions.exp: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂; P₂ = (2×10⁵ × 4.0)/2.0 = 4.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

questions.q: Under which conditions does a real gas deviate most from ideal behaviour?
questions.exp: At high P, particle volumes matter; at low T, intermolecular forces become significant.

questions.q: What is the relationship between average kinetic energy and temperature?
opts: Average KE ∝ absolute temperature (T in K)
questions.exp: A fundamental assumption of kinetic theory: average molecular KE is proportional to absolute temperature.

questions.q: Which correctly states Charles's law?
opts: V/T = constant at constant P (T in K)
questions.exp: Charles's law: at constant pressure, V is proportional to absolute temperature.

questions.q: What does the ideal gas equation assume about intermolecular forces?
opts: There are no intermolecular forces between gas molecules
They only exist between polar molecules
questions.exp: An ideal gas is modelled as point masses with no intermolecular forces. Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour when intermolecular forces become significant — at low temperatures and high pressures.

questions.q: At constant temperature, halving the volume of an ideal gas will:
questions.exp: Boyle's law: P ∝ 1/V at constant T and n. If V is halved, P doubles (PV = constant). The molecules collide with the walls twice as frequently in the smaller volume.

questions.q: What is the molar volume of an ideal gas at RTP (25 °C, 100 kPa)?
questions.exp: At RTP (25 °C, 100 kPa), the molar volume is 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹. The old STP value (0 °C, 1 atm) is 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹. Cambridge A Level uses RTP = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: In a gas at constant volume, increasing temperature causes:
opts: Pressure to decrease because molecules slow down
Pressure to increase because molecules move faster and collide more frequently with more force
Volume to increase to maintain pressure
No change — only volume can change with temperature
questions.exp: At constant volume, the molecules cannot expand. Higher temperature → higher average kinetic energy → more frequent collisions with the container walls AND with greater force → pressure increases (Gay-Lussac's law: P ∝ T at constant V).

questions.q: Which of these is a property of a giant covalent (network) solid?
opts: Very high melting point, does not conduct electricity (except graphite)
questions.exp: Giant covalent solids (diamond, SiO₂, SiC) have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken. Most are non-conductors (except graphite, which has delocalised electrons). They are insoluble in most solvents.

questions.q: Which intermolecular force is present in ALL molecular substances?
questions.exp: London (van der Waals) forces arise from temporary, instantaneous dipoles due to uneven electron distribution. They exist in ALL molecules — polar or non-polar, large or small. Other forces (H-bonding, dipole–dipole) exist only in specific molecules.

questions.q: Use PV = nRT to find the pressure (Pa) of 0.50 mol ideal gas at 300 K in 10 L (0.010 m³). R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Why do noble gases (e.g. Ar, Kr) have higher boiling points with increasing atomic number?
opts: Larger atoms have more electrons → stronger London forces → more energy needed to boil
questions.exp: Noble gases are monatomic with only London forces between atoms. Larger atoms (more electrons) have greater polarisability — temporary dipoles are larger and induced more easily. Stronger London forces → higher boiling point.

questions.q: Real gases deviate most from ideal behaviour at:
questions.exp: At low temperature, molecules move slowly and intermolecular attractions become significant (ignored in ideal model). At high pressure, molecules are close together and their own volume is no longer negligible. Both effects cause real deviation from ideal.

questions.q: Which substance has the highest melting point?
questions.exp: SiO₂ (quartz/silica) is a giant covalent network solid — melting it requires breaking millions of strong Si–O covalent bonds (mp ~1710 °C). NaCl melts at ~801 °C. H₂O at 0 °C. I₂ at ~114 °C.

questions.q: Which gas law states that at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional?
questions.exp: Boyle's law: P ∝ 1/V at constant T. If volume halves, pressure doubles.

questions.q: The ideal gas equation is PV = nRT. What are the units of R?
questions.exp: R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Since P is in Pa (= J m⁻³) and V in m³, R = PV/nT has units J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

questions.q: 0.5 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K and 1×10⁵ Pa. What is its volume?
At which conditions do real gases deviate most from ideal behaviour?
questions.exp: At high pressure, particle volumes become significant. At low temperature, intermolecular forces are significant. Both cause deviation from PV = nRT.

questions.q: Why do noble gases behave most like ideal gases?
opts: They are monatomic with negligible intermolecular forces
They do not follow Boyle's law
questions.exp: Noble gases have no dipole, no hydrogen bonds, and very weak id–id forces — their behaviour closely matches the ideal gas assumptions.

questions.q: What is the molar volume of an ideal gas at RTP (25°C, 100 kPa)?
questions.exp: At RTP (298 K, 100 kPa): V = RT/P = 8.31 × 298 / 100000 = 0.0248 m³ = 24.8 dm³. The commonly used value is 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ (approximated).

questions.q: The pressure in a fixed-volume container increases when temperature rises because:
opts: Average kinetic energy increases so collisions are more frequent and energetic
questions.exp: Higher T → higher average Ek → more frequent collisions with walls and greater force per collision → higher pressure (Gay-Lussac's law: P ∝ T at constant V).

questions.q: In a giant covalent structure like diamond, why is the melting point extremely high?
opts: Many strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice that all must be broken
questions.exp: Diamond has a 3D network of strong C–C covalent bonds throughout. Melting requires breaking all these bonds — requires enormous energy.

questions.q: Which state of matter has definite volume but no definite shape?
questions.exp: A liquid has a fixed volume (incompressible) but takes the shape of its container. Solids have fixed shape and volume; gases have neither.

questions.q: Intermolecular forces in liquids are responsible for:
questions.exp: Intermolecular forces hold liquid molecules close together, giving rise to surface tension (minimising surface area) and viscosity (resistance to flow).

recall: State the assumptions of the kinetic theory.
State and use the ideal gas equation.
Explain why real gases deviate from ideal at high pressure.
Use Boyle's and Charles's law to solve problems.
Explain the difference between gas, liquid and solid in terms of particle arrangement and forces.
